summary: Year 3 learners (age 7–8) total two or three items priced in pounds and pence, give change from a £5 or £10 note, and record amounts correctly (e.g. £3.47). The reliable route to change from a note is counting UP from the total spent to the note (finding the difference), not column subtraction across zeros. The central hazard is treating £.p as two separate whole numbers ('string-length thinking'); learners must exchange 100p for £1 and treat each amount as one quantity. Note: the National Curriculum's non-statutory notes and guidance for Year 3 say pupils record £ and p separately, and formal decimal recording of money is introduced in Year 4, so teach the £3.47 form carefully alongside its pence-and-pounds meaning.
misconceptions: 'String-length thinking' — treats £ and p as two separate whole numbers (adds the pence column past 100 without exchanging, or writes £3.7 for £3 and 70p).
Notation errors — omits the decimal point, mixes units (£3.47p), or writes pence as if pounds.
Attempts change from £10 by column subtraction and makes 'take smaller from larger' / subtract-across-zeros errors instead of counting up.
'Most coins = most money' persists, and reading '£2.47' as 'two point forty-seven' reinforces the two-separate-numbers error.

activities.title: Shop till: total, pay, and count change up
steps: Choose two or three priced items (e.g. a £2.60 car and a £1.85 book) and total them, building the total step by step (£2.60 + £1.85 = £4.45).
Pay with a £5 note and work out the change by counting UP from the total to the note, drawing each jump on an empty number line: £4.45 → +5p → £4.50 → +50p → £5.00, so change is 55p.
Collect the change as actual coins into a tray; when the pennies/pence in the tray reach 100p, physically exchange them for a single £1 coin and re-read the amount as one quantity.
Repeat for a single £3.47 item paid with a £5 note: count up £3.47 → £3.50 → £4.00 → £5.00 = £1.53.

Record the change in £ and p notation (e.g. £0.55, 55p), then say the amount in a place-value-honest way suitable for Year 3 (e.g. 'fifty-five pence'); avoid reading the pence as a compound whole number joined to the pounds (e.g. 'three point forty-seven' for £3.47). Reading the digits separately ('nought point five five') is also acceptable and is the decimal reading the cited research recommends.
activities.insight: Change from a note is a short counting-on jump from the total to the note, and an amount in pounds and pence is ONE quantity because 100p exchanges for £1.

activities.title: Record it right: correct versus incorrect money notation
steps: For a given amount of coins in a tray, write the amount in £ and p and check it against the coins.
Compare correct and incorrect recordings side by side (e.g. £0.55 vs £0.55p vs £55) and decide which one matches the coins, explaining how you know.
Record the same amount in more than one correct way where sensible (e.g. 55p and £0.55) and explain they are equal.
Practise see–say–record: see the coins, say the amount place-value-honestly, then write it without ever joining £ and p (never £3.47p).
activities.insight: Money notation carries meaning: the decimal point separates pounds from pence, £ and p are never written together, and the written amount must match the value of the coins.

activities.title: Estimate first, then check for sense
steps: Before calculating change, estimate: 'I spent about £4.50, so the change should be small.'
After finding change, compare it with the estimate and say whether the answer is reasonable.
Verify change by counting it back onto the total to rebuild the note.
When paying with a £10 note instead of £5, predict how the change will differ and decide whether counting up or column subtraction would be easier.
activities.insight: Estimating before calculating catches unreasonable answers, and change from a note can always be checked by rebuilding the note.

activities.title: Quick checks on notation and reasonableness
steps: Fill in the blank to record a shown amount in correct £ and p notation.
Choose which of several written forms correctly records a given amount (e.g. £3.47 among £347 and £3.47p, with the incorrect forms clearly present only as non-examples to be rejected).
Choose or state the correct change for a simple purchase from a note.
Put a set of money amounts in order from least to most to practise treating each as one quantity.
activities.insight: Correct notation and reasonable amounts can be recognised and chosen reliably once the single-quantity meaning is understood.

activities.title: Shopkeeper role-play to narrate the method (optional support)
steps: Take the role of shopkeeper and, out loud, talk a 'customer' through giving change: name the total, then count up from the total to the note coin by coin.
Explain aloud why 100p becomes £1 while handing over the change.
activities.insight: Verbalising the counting-on method and the 100p→£1 exchange may help a learner articulate and consolidate the procedure.

checkQuestion: Give the child a small shop of priced items and real/realistic coins and notes. Say: 'Buy the £2.60 car and the £1.85 book. Pay with this £5 note, work out the change, and write down the change using £ and p.' Then: 'Now buy just the £3.47 game and pay with a £5 note — what's the change?' Watch the method and the notation, not only the final number.
checkAnswer: Totals £2.60 + £1.85 = £4.45; finds change by counting up £4.45 → £4.50 → £5.00 = 55p (or column subtraction done correctly with exchange), and records it as £0.55 / 55p in consistent notation. For the game: £5.00 − £3.47 = £1.53, again best reached by counting on. Treats each amount as one quantity, exchanging 100p for £1 where needed.
